newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche-won't shed stakes unless taxes are cut.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche-won't shed stakes unless taxes are cut.

text.p: Deutsche Bank AG's outgoing chief executive Hilmar Kopper on Tuesday reiterated that the bank has no plans to shed its industrial shareholdings unless corporate taxes are lowered.
"Our position on this has not changed," Kopper told shareholders at the bank's annual general meeting (AGM).
"For tax reasons there is absolutely no reason to realise our hidden reserves. If the tax regime changes, the management board will consider it."
Kopper, who moves up into the bank's non-executive supervisory board after the AGM, will be succeeded by Rolf Breuer, an investment banking specialist who has been on the management board since 1985.

Kopper was speaking after Breuer was quoted in the Financial Times as saying Deutsche planned to reduce its German industrial shareholdings to achieve a balance between its domestic and international holdings.
But Breuer, reiterating the bank's standard line, said this depended on how quickly taxes would be cut and that the reduction in shareholdings would probably not happen until the next century.

Deutsche has large holdings in German industrial companies including a 22.6 percent stake in Daimler-Benz AG and 10 percent in insurer Allianz AG Holding, and could cause steep declines in the share prices of those companies if it offloaded its stakes in one fell swoop.
Its stakes also include 25.8 percent of builder Philip Holzmann AG, Deutz AG, 10 percent of Munich Reinsurance and 10.2 percent of Continental AG.

The bank has been steadily reducing its stakes for example by not participating in capital increases. The stake in Daimler has been gradually cut from 28 percent and Deutsche has also reduced its stake in department store group Karstadt AG.

Analysts said a reduction in shareholdings would release funds which could be more profitably invested elsewhere. It would also dampen public criticism of the power banks wield through their holdings, which give them many seats on company supervisory boards.

In addition, banks no longer require large stakes to underpin their traditional banking relationships with large companies, a business field that has become less important as a source of income, analysts said.

"Deutsche is investing heavily and must recoup the costs," said Stefan Ermisch, banking analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank. "It has big potential to realise gains. But any reduction in stakes will be gradual."
Dieter Hein, banking analyst at BHF-Bank, said "It makes sense that to reduce shareholdings which are not strategically necessary and cause trouble."
Analysts said Deutsche would reduce its stakes bit by bit even without a major cut in corporate tax but that big sell-offs were unlikely unless taxes are reduced.
When that will happen remains unclear.

The ruling government coalition plans to slash corporate income tax to 35 percent from 47 percent as part of a broad tax reform to cut the overall tax burden by a net 30 billion marks ($17.7 billion).

Part of the reforms, in particular the corporate tax cuts, were due to take effect in 1998 but the entire reform package is in limbo at present amid political wrangling between the coalition and the opposition Social Democrats, who can block any tax changes through their control of the Bundesrat, or upper house of the federal parliament.
Deutsche's Frankfurt rival Dresdner Bank AG on Tuesday declined to comment on its stake plans.
Commerzbank AG said it could imagine selling stakes when the opportunity arose but that its holdings were not on the scale of Deutsche's.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.695 German Marks)
